<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and rhetorically strong, but A (CON) did more decisive rebuttal work and ended with more live, unanswered offense. A's mechanistic case — appropriations lose annual budget fights while term contracts deliver attached revenue — survived the exchange: B's political-will tu quoque ("if a city can police a lease, it can pass a levy") was answered by A's frequency asymmetry ("permanent victory vs. one victory and a filing cabinet"), which B never countered. B also repeated the streets analogy in Rebuttal 2 after A had collapsed it (meters, tolls, congestion charges), leaving a damaging point untouched. A's failure-mode weighing (partial/visible/reversible rope vs. total/invisible closure) was effectively conceded as a frame by B ("fiscal starvation is a political choice, same as enclosure") and then exploited. B's closing capture ("they have given the case away") was punchy but overstated — A still defended ticketed decks/rinks/wheels, squarely within the motion's "paid private experiences" language, and A's closing exposed B's own softening on edge decks. B's values case (second rent, citizens not customers) was forceful but comparatively asserted rather than weighed at the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.2 collapsing B's streets/sewers analogy by showing "free at the curb is underwritten by charges" (meters, tolls, congestion zones) — never answered — compounded by A4.4's frequency asymmetry neutralizing B's strongest counter, the political-will tu quoque.</best_rebuttal>
